faq.q: Why do bathrooms need an extractor fan?
faq.a: Showers and baths fill the air with water vapour. Without a fan it condenses on cold surfaces, causing peeling paint and mould, so the fan carries the damp air outside.
asks: Why does my bathroom get mouldy?

faq.q: How does a fan know the bathroom is steamy?
faq.a: Some fans have a humidity sensor that switches them on when the air gets damp and off when it dries. Others simply run with the light, often with a timer.

faq.q: Why does a fan keep running after I leave?
faq.a: A built-in timer keeps it going for several minutes so it can clear the steam that is still in the room after you switch off the light.
asks: Why does my bathroom fan not stop straight away?

faq.q: Why is there a gap under the bathroom door?
faq.a: An extractor can only push air out if fresh air can get in. The gap lets drier air from the house replace the air the fan removes.
asks: Why should I leave the bathroom door slightly open?

faq.q: Why do kitchens have extractor hoods?
faq.a: Cooking releases steam, grease and smells. A hood above the hob catches them, filters grease and often blows the air outside.
asks: What does a cooker hood do?

facts: Building rules in England expect an intermittent bathroom extractor to move at least 15 litres of air per second.
Water vapour condenses on surfaces colder than the air, which is why mirrors mist up first.
